page.text:
While the integers $\mathbb{Z}$ resolve the asymmetry of subtraction in
the natural numbers, they remain closed under division only in
exceptional circumstances: equations of the form $b \cdot x = a$ with
$b \neq 0$ admit solutions in $\mathbb{Z}$ if and only if $b$ divides
$a$. To endow our arithmetic universe with complete division by nonzero
quantities, we must construct the field of fractions $\mathbb{Q}$.

Geometrically and physically, rational numbers correspond to ratios of
commensurable magnitudes—fractions of an indivisible unit measure.
Algebraically, they represent the smallest field containing the integral
domain $\mathbb{Z}$. Abstractly, $\mathbb{Q}$ forms an ordered field in
which addition and multiplication interact via distributivity, every
nonzero element possesses a unique multiplicative inverse, and the order
$\leq$ respects translation and scaling by positive elements. Concretely,
a rational number is represented by a pair
$(a, b) \in \mathbb{Z} \times (\mathbb{Z} \setminus \{0\})$, interpreted
as $a/b$, where two formal quotients $a/b$ and $c/d$ designate the same
rational quantity precisely when their cross-products coincide:
$ad = bc$.
